screens.title: Introduction to Load Balancing
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will build a clear mental model of load balancing and why it is central to modern, resilient systems. Load balancing distributes incoming client requests across a pool of backend servers so no single server becomes a bottleneck. That is what keeps large applications responsive at traffic peaks and allows maintenance without downtime. We’ll use a simple analogy: a traffic cop directing vehicles to multiple lanes so no single lane gets jammed. You’ll hear concrete examples such as an e-commerce site where a single web server would slow or crash under peak load. We also explain the most common algorithms — round robin, least connection, and IP hash — and when each shines. Finally, we introduce the two Red Hat–centric tools you should know: HAProxy, the high-performance workhorse that distributes traffic and handles health checks, and Keepalived, which manages a floating IP to prevent the load balancer itself from becoming a single point of failure. By the end of this chapter you’ll understand the distinct roles these tools play and the basic algorithm choices an architect must make. Think about a peak sale event: how would you keep pages fast and available? That question guides our practical examples ahead.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Introduction to Load Balancing
Introduction to Load Balancing
Distribute requests, improve scalability, and keep services responsive under load.

Load balancing prevents any single backend from being overwhelmed. It is a fundamental design pattern for horizontally scalable systems and pairs naturally with high-availability techniques to reduce downtime.

In this lesson
Why LB matters

Scalability, performance, maintenance

Algorithms

Round Robin, Least Connection, IP Hash

Red Hat tools

HAProxy & Keepalived roles

Visual concept
Load balancer directs traffic to a backend pool; VIP protects the entry point
HAProxy
Handles TCP/HTTP distribution, health checks, SSL offload, and content routing. Optimized for many concurrent connections.
Operates at Layer 4 and Layer 7
Keepalived
Manages a floating VIP via VRRP so the load balancer itself stays available during failover.
Think of HAProxy as the traffic cop and Keepalived as the backup radio that hands the badge to the next officer when one goes offline.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Foundations
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives give you a practical map for learning load balancing in a Red Hat environment. First, you will define load balancing and explain why it is essential for distributed systems, including how it differs from and complements high availability. For example, you will be able to describe how a traffic cop analogy maps to backend pools and response times. Second, you will identify common load balancing algorithms and the specific situations where each is preferable. You will use concrete examples such as sequential Round Robin, Least Connection when session lengths vary, and IP Hash for session persistence. Third, you will understand the tangible benefits: how load balancing improves scalability by allowing horizontal server growth, increases reliability by removing failed backends from rotation, and boosts performance by spreading work. Fourth, you will be introduced to Red Hat’s primary tools — HAProxy and Keepalived — and be able to explain their distinct roles. Each objective is tied to a competency milestone so you can verify mastery by explaining an architecture where HAProxy distributes traffic and Keepalived manages the VIP.

screens.title: What is Load Balancing?
screens.narratorSegment: Load balancing is the deliberate distribution of client requests across multiple backend servers so that no single server is overloaded. It differs from infrastructure-level high availability, which focuses on recovery and redundancy; load balancing distributes work at the application layer while high availability minimizes downtime. A useful analogy is a traffic cop directing cars to several lanes: the cop doesn’t make cars faster, but by spreading them across lanes all cars move more smoothly. Concretely, an e-commerce storefront without a load balancer routes every user to the same server. That server can become a bottleneck at peak traffic and the user experience slows or fails. With a load balancer, the client-facing endpoint remains stable while the balancer forwards each request to a healthy backend. Important subtleties are that load balancing can also perform SSL termination, health checks, and content-based routing; these features let the balancer act as a first line of policy and performance optimization. A common misconception is that load balancing alone solves every availability problem; it does not replace proper redundancy and recovery mechanisms. Your takeaway: load balancing reduces single-server bottlenecks and enables horizontal growth, but it must be paired with health checks and redundancy to create resilient systems.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › What is Load Balancing?
Definition and analogy

Load balancing evenly distributes requests across a backend pool so individual servers avoid overload. Think of it as a traffic cop who guides vehicles into multiple lanes so no lane becomes jammed. The stable client-facing endpoint stays constant while the balancer forwards each request to the most appropriate backend.

Key role

Responsiveness and distribution

Complementary to HA

Works with recovery and redundancy

Key Takeaway

Load balancing reduces single-server bottlenecks and enables horizontal scaling; combine it with health checks and redundancy for resilience.

Concrete example
An online store with a single server slows during a sale. Add a load balancer and two additional servers. The client endpoint stays the same; the balancer distributes requests so each server handles fewer concurrent sessions, improving response times.
Common misconception
Some assume load balancing alone guarantees availability. It improves distribution, but without health checks and redundant infrastructure the system can still fail if backends or the balancer itself go down.

screens.title: Benefits of Load Balancing
screens.narratorSegment: Load balancing delivers several practical benefits that matter to architects and operators. First, scalability: by routing requests to a backend pool you enable horizontal scaling — add servers under the same client endpoint without changing DNS or clients. Second, reliability and high availability: the load balancer can perform health checks and stop sending traffic to failed instances, which keeps services available even when individual servers fail. Third, performance: distributing requests reduces per-server load, which shortens response times and improves throughput. Fourth, flexibility: load balancers can terminate SSL, route based on URLs or headers, and perform application-level checks, which centralizes operational policies. Fifth, maintenance becomes easier because servers can be taken out of rotation for upgrades while the load balancer continues to serve traffic from healthy nodes. An important operational note is that these benefits depend on good health checks and correct algorithm selection; a misconfigured health check or a poor algorithm choice can negate the advantages. For practical review, maintain a checklist to confirm horizontal scaling paths, health checks, graceful maintenance flows, and whether SSL termination or content routing should live on the balancer.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Benefits of Load Balancing
Scalability
Add backend servers to handle more requests without changing the client endpoint.
Reliability & HA
Health checks remove failed servers from rotation so clients still reach healthy instances.
Performance
Distributing work lowers per-server load and shortens response times.
Operational details and checklist
  • Confirm health checks are realistic and detect application faults, not just OS reachability.
  • Decide where SSL termination should occur and document certificate management policies.
  • Select algorithms that match traffic patterns and server capacity; test with realistic loads.
  • Plan maintenance flows: drain connections from a server before taking it offline.
Key Takeaway

Benefits depend on correct health checks, algorithm choice, and operational procedures. Load balancing is powerful when paired with monitoring and redundancy.

screens.title: Load Balancing Algorithms
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing a load balancing algorithm shapes how requests land on backends and directly affects fairness and responsiveness. The main algorithms to know are Round Robin, Weighted Round Robin, Least Connection, Weighted Least Connection, IP Hash, and Least Time. Round Robin cycles requests sequentially through servers; it is simple and effective when servers are similar. Weighted Round Robin assigns more requests to stronger servers by giving them higher weights. Least Connection sends new requests to the server with the fewest active connections, which helps when requests vary in duration. Weighted Least Connection applies weights to that same idea. IP Hash computes a hash of the client’s IP so that the same client tends to reach the same server, which can provide session persistence without application cookies. Least Time is an advanced option that considers both response time and active connections to pick the fastest server. Use the three-server exercise from the chapter to practice: with servers handling 70, 30, and 50 active requests respectively, ask where the next five requests go under Round Robin versus Least Connection. A typical misconception is assuming Round Robin is always fair; it ignores current load and long-lived connections, which can make it unsuitable for heterogeneous or variable workloads. Your job as an architect is to match observed traffic patterns with the algorithm’s strengths and limitations.

keyIdea.text: Match the algorithm to traffic patterns: Round Robin for uniform load, Least Connection for variable-duration requests, and IP Hash when session persistence is needed.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Load Balancing Algorithms
Algorithm quick reference
Round Robin

Sequential, simple, good for similar servers

Weighted RR

More traffic to stronger servers

Least Connection

Sends to fewest active connections

IP Hash

Client affinity by IP

Least Time

Advanced: considers response time and connection count

Hands-on scenario
Servers A, B, and C can each handle 100 requests per second. Current load: A=70, B=30, C=50 active requests. If five more requests arrive, under Round Robin they go to the next servers in sequence without regard to load; under Least Connection they will prefer servers with fewer active connections, so B and C are more likely to receive the new requests until loads rebalance.
Common misconception
Equating fairness with Round Robin is misleading. Fair distribution of work depends on request duration and server capacity; Round Robin ignores those factors.

screens.title: Round Robin and Weighted Variants
screens.narratorSegment: Round Robin is one of the simplest load balancing strategies: forward each incoming request to the next server in the pool in a fixed sequence. Its simplicity is an advantage when servers are similar, but it ignores current load and request duration. Weighted Round Robin refines this by assigning weights to servers; a server with weight two receives twice as many requests as a server with weight one. Consider the chapter scenario where Server B is upgraded to handle more capacity — under Weighted Round Robin you would give B a higher weight so it receives proportionally more traffic. When assigning weights, base them on measurable capacity metrics such as C P U, memory, or network throughput. A common pitfall is choosing weights by gut feel rather than metrics, which can create imbalances. Another misconception is assuming Weighted Round Robin solves variable request durations — it helps for static capacity differences but still does not react to real-time connection counts or slow-running requests. For workloads with long-lived or highly variable requests, algorithms that consider active connections or response time are often better. Practice: pick capacity numbers for servers A, B, and C and calculate the assignment of the next 15 requests under Weighted Round Robin to confirm the expected distribution.

keyIdea.text: Round Robin is straightforward; weighted variants distribute more traffic to stronger servers but still do not adapt to sudden load spikes or long-lived connections.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Round Robin & Weighted
How it works
Round Robin sends each request to the next server in order. Weighted Round Robin multiplies that sequence by each server's weight so more capable servers receive more traffic.
  1. Assign weights based on measured capacity, not guesswork.
  2. Calculate distribution using the weight ratio to predict traffic splits.
  3. Monitor real traffic to confirm expected behavior and adjust as needed.
Concrete example
If A and C have weight 1 and B has weight 1.5 or 2 after an upgrade, B will receive more requests. For fifteen incoming requests, compute assignments using the weights to confirm expected counts per server.
Pitfall
Weighted Round Robin does not account for current active connections or response latency. If requests vary widely in processing time, prefer connection-aware algorithms.

screens.title: Least Connection and Advanced Variants
screens.narratorSegment: Least Connection algorithms route new requests to the backend with the fewest active connections. This is especially useful when requests have variable durations or when a server may be temporarily slower. Weighted Least Connection adds server capacity into the decision so faster backends still get more traffic but decisions remain informed by current load. Least Time is a more advanced choice: it factors in both active connections and measured response times to estimate which server will finish fastest for a new request. Why does this matter? In real-world services some requests are quick and some long-running; a purely sequential approach can overload a server processing many long requests. Least Connection dynamically compensates for that by steering new arrivals to less-busy servers. A common misconception is that counting connections equals perfect load measurement; long-lived idle connections can distort the view, and connection count doesn't capture C P U or input and output saturation. Always combine these algorithms with good health checks and real metrics like response latency and server utilization. A practical exercise is to simulate variable-duration requests and observe how Least Connection rebalances more effectively than Round Robin in that scenario.

keyIdea.title: Connection-aware balancing
keyIdea.text: Least Connection and its weighted/least-time variants react to current load and response time, making them better for variable-duration or heterogeneous workloads.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Least Connection & Variants
What it measures
Least Connection tracks active sessions. Weighted Least Connection adds server capacity into the decision. Least Time combines active connections with measured response time to pick the fastest candidate.
When to choose these: services with highly variable request duration, mixed server capabilities, or frequent long-running requests that would unfairly skew simple sequenced algorithms.
Example exercise
Simulate several short requests and a few long requests. Observe how Least Connection routes new arrivals away from servers handling the long tasks, keeping overall latency lower for new clients.
Misconception
Connection count alone can be misleading if many connections are idle or if CPU is saturated. Combine with latency and utilization metrics for a more accurate picture.

screens.title: IP Hash and Session Persistence
screens.narratorSegment: IP Hash uses the client’s source IP address to compute a deterministic mapping to a backend server, providing a simple form of session persistence often called sticky sessions. This is useful when you need a client to reach the same server across multiple requests but cannot rely on application-level cookies. For example, a legacy web application that stores session state in local memory benefits from IP Hash because it keeps a client bound to a single backend. However, there are important limitations: clients behind NAT or large-scale proxies may share public IP addresses so affinity can become coarse or incorrect. Also, IP-based mapping can prevent even distribution when client IPs cluster in ranges. A common misconception is that IP Hash is universally superior for persistence; in practice it is a tradeoff that works well for straightforward topologies but not for complex, multi-tiered deployments or widespread NAT. When persistence is needed at scale, architects often use centralized session stores or application-level mechanisms combined with cookie-based affinity. The key is to weigh the simplicity of IP Hash against its affinity limitations in your environment.

keyIdea.text: IP Hash provides deterministic client affinity using the source IP, useful for simple persistence but limited by NAT and shared IP scenarios.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › IP Hash & Persistence
How IP Hash works
The balancer computes a hash of the client IP and maps that hash to a backend. The same client IP will map to the same backend consistently, enabling sticky sessions without application cookies.
When to use it: simple topologies where clients have stable public IPs and session persistence is needed. When not to use it: when many clients share IPs via NAT, or where IP ranges are unevenly distributed.
Concrete example
A legacy app with in-memory sessions can use IP Hash to keep a user on the same server without changing the app to use a shared session store.
Limitation
Shared IPs and NAT can break the usefulness of IP Hash. In such environments prefer explicit session stores or cookie-based affinity.

screens.title: HAProxy: the high-performance workhorse
screens.narratorSegment: HAProxy is a high-performance, open-source proxy and load balancer used widely in Red Hat environments. It handles both Layer 4 (TCP) and Layer 7 (HTTP) traffic, making it flexible for many workloads. HAProxy performs core functions such as connection multiplexing, application-layer health checks, SSL offloading, sticky sessions, and content-based routing. Architects pick HAProxy when they need a reliable, configurable component that can handle a large number of concurrent connections with predictable behavior. Typical deployments put HAProxy in front of web servers, application servers, or even databases, with backends forming a server farm. Important operational considerations include tuning for maximum connections, configuring appropriate health checks to detect real failures, and planning certificate management for SSL termination. A misconception is that HAProxy is only useful for HTTP; it is equally effective for TCP-based applications. When combined with a VIP manager such as Keepalived, HAProxy forms the distribution layer while Keepalived ensures the load balancer endpoint remains available. Practice sketching a deployment where HAProxy routes traffic to three app servers and performs an HTTP health check with a short interval so you can see how it removes unhealthy nodes quickly.

keyIdea.text: HAProxy distributes TCP/HTTP traffic, performs health checks and advanced routing, and scales to many concurrent connections, making it a common choice for Red Hat architectures.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › HAProxy Overview
Capabilities
  • Layer 4 and Layer 7 load balancing for TCP and HTTP applications.
  • Health checks that remove unhealthy servers from rotation automatically.
  • SSL offloading and content-based routing for flexible traffic policies.
  • High concurrency with tunable connection limits and timeouts.
Typical use cases
Fronting web servers, application servers, or databases where efficient, configurable traffic distribution is required.
Misconception
HAProxy is not limited to HTTP. It also handles TCP workloads effectively and is chosen for its performance across protocols.

screens.title: Keepalived: VIP management with VRRP
screens.narratorSegment: Keepalived is a routing software suite commonly used to provide high availability for Linux hosts by managing a floating Virtual IP address. Its most important role in a load balancing architecture is to prevent the load balancer itself from becoming a single point of failure. Keepalived uses the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol to elect an active node that owns the VIP; when that node fails, Keepalived moves the VIP to a standby node. In practical deployments, HAProxy runs on both the primary and standby hosts, each capable of handling traffic. keyIdea.title: Keepalived role
keyIdea.text: Keepalived manages a floating VIP via VRRP to move client traffic to a standby load balancer when the primary fails, preventing the load balancer from being a single point of failure.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Keepalived & VRRP
What Keepalived does
Keepalived provides a floating Virtual IP and implements VRRP to move that IP from a failed primary to a standby. This ensures the client-facing address remains available even when the active load balancer fails.
Keepalived can also coordinate basic Layer 4 services with LVS, but its most critical role in LB stacks is VIP failover for HAProxy or similar balancers.
Failover sequence
Primary holds VIP; Keepalived monitors. If the primary fails or signals an issue, VRRP elects a standby to take the VIP, and clients reconnect to the standby without changing the IP they use.
Operational note
Test VIP movement and connection draining policies so in-flight sessions behave acceptably during failover. Treat Keepalived as the VIP manager, not the application health authority.

screens.title: HAProxy and Keepalived Together
screens.narratorSegment: In production Red Hat architectures you’ll commonly see HAProxy and Keepalived deployed together. HAProxy performs the traffic distribution to backend servers, handling Layer 4 and 7 tasks and application-aware health checks. Keepalived manages a floating virtual IP via VRRP so the HAProxy service itself does not become a single point of failure. The combined pattern is straightforward: configure two or more HAProxy instances, have Keepalived manage a VIP on the active instance, and ensure HAProxy and Keepalived health checks are coordinated. If the active HAProxy host fails, Keepalived moves the VIP to a standby host, and that host’s HAProxy immediately begins accepting traffic. Important deployment practices include enabling graceful connection draining so the active instance finishes in-flight requests before stepping down, aligning health-check thresholds so Keepalived does not shift VIPs for transient conditions, and monitoring both application-level and host-level metrics. A common mistake is to assume VIP movement alone guarantees application-level health; always ensure HAProxy is configured to detect backend failures so it stops sending traffic to unhealthy servers even while the VIP remains active. Your architecture review checklist should include VIP failover tests, draining behavior, and synchronized health checks across the stack.

keyIdea.title: Combined pattern
keyIdea.text: Pair HAProxy for distribution with Keepalived for VIP failover, coordinate health checks and graceful draining to achieve a resilient load balancing layer.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › HAProxy + Keepalived
Typical deployment pattern
Two HAProxy nodes run in active/standby. Keepalived manages a VIP so clients always connect to the same IP. HAProxy performs health checks and distributes traffic to backend servers. On primary failure, Keepalived migrates the VIP to the standby, which accepts connections immediately.
Ensure draining and coordinated health checks so sessions complete gracefully and VIP moves only when the host truly cannot serve traffic.
Scenario: maintenance
Drain the primary HAProxy, remove the VIP, perform maintenance, then return the VIP. Clients experience no DNS change and traffic continues via the standby while you maintain the primary.
Common mistake
Relying solely on VIP failover without HAProxy-level health checks can let unhealthy backends continue receiving traffic. Coordinate both layers for resilience.

That trio helps you translate these concepts into architecture diagrams and operational checklists. Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Key Concepts — Algorithms & Tools
Round Robin
Sequential distribution; simple but ignores current load.
Least Connection
Routes to the server with the fewest active connections; better for variable-duration workloads.
IP Hash
Provides deterministic client affinity by hashing source IP; useful but limited when NAT is present.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will build a clear mental model of load balancing and why it is central to modern, resilient systems. Load balancing distributes incoming client requests across a pool of backend servers so no single server becomes a bottleneck. That is what keeps large applications responsive at traffic peaks and allows maintenance without downtime. We’ll use a simple analogy: a traffic cop directing vehicles to multiple lanes so no single lane gets jammed. You’ll hear concrete examples such as an e-commerce site where a single web server would slow or crash under peak load. We also explain the most common algorithms — round robin, least connection, and IP hash — and when each shines. Finally, we introduce the two Red Hat–centric tools you should know: HAProxy, the high-performance workhorse that distributes traffic and handles health checks, and Keepalived, which manages a floating IP to prevent the load balancer itself from becoming a single point of failure. By the end of this chapter you’ll understand the distinct roles these tools play and the basic algorithm choices an architect must make. Think about a peak sale event: how would you keep pages fast and available? That question guides our practical examples ahead.

These four objectives give you a practical map for learning load balancing in a Red Hat environment. First, you will define load balancing and explain why it is essential for distributed systems, including how it differs from and complements high availability. For example, you will be able to describe how a traffic cop analogy maps to backend pools and response times. Second, you will identify common load balancing algorithms and the specific situations where each is preferable. You will use concrete examples such as sequential Round Robin, Least Connection when session lengths vary, and IP Hash for session persistence. Third, you will understand the tangible benefits: how load balancing improves scalability by allowing horizontal server growth, increases reliability by removing failed backends from rotation, and boosts performance by spreading work. Fourth, you will be introduced to Red Hat’s primary tools — HAProxy and Keepalived — and be able to explain their distinct roles. Each objective is tied to a competency milestone so you can verify mastery by explaining an architecture where HAProxy distributes traffic and Keepalived manages the VIP.

This second objectives slide translates definitions into practical milestones you can demonstrate. For definition and difference from HA, practice by explaining a failure scenario where a backend crashes and showing how a load balancer reroutes traffic without changing the client endpoint. For algorithms, practice by taking the three-server scenario in the chapter and predicting where the next five requests land under Round Robin and Least Connection. For benefits, build a short checklist you can apply during architecture reviews: will the design allow horizontal scaling, remove failed servers automatically, and support maintenance without downtime? Finally, for Red Hat tools, sketch a two-node HAProxy pair and add Keepalived managing a VIP; describe the failover sequence initiated by VRRP. Each card on this screen pairs a competency description with a small mnemonic so you can quickly test your understanding during design reviews or interviews.

Load balancing is the deliberate distribution of client requests across multiple backend servers so that no single server is overloaded. It differs from infrastructure-level high availability, which focuses on recovery and redundancy; load balancing distributes work at the application layer while high availability minimizes downtime. A useful analogy is a traffic cop directing cars to several lanes: the cop doesn’t make cars faster, but by spreading them across lanes all cars move more smoothly. Concretely, an e-commerce storefront without a load balancer routes every user to the same server. That server can become a bottleneck at peak traffic and the user experience slows or fails. With a load balancer, the client-facing endpoint remains stable while the balancer forwards each request to a healthy backend. Important subtleties are that load balancing can also perform SSL termination, health checks, and content-based routing; these features let the balancer act as a first line of policy and performance optimization. A common misconception is that load balancing alone solves every availability problem; it does not replace proper redundancy and recovery mechanisms. Your takeaway: load balancing reduces single-server bottlenecks and enables horizontal growth, but it must be paired with health checks and redundancy to create resilient systems.

Load balancing delivers several practical benefits that matter to architects and operators. First, scalability: by routing requests to a backend pool you enable horizontal scaling — add servers under the same client endpoint without changing DNS or clients. Second, reliability and high availability: the load balancer can perform health checks and stop sending traffic to failed instances, which keeps services available even when individual servers fail. Third, performance: distributing requests reduces per-server load, which shortens response times and improves throughput. Fourth, flexibility: load balancers can terminate SSL, route based on URLs or headers, and perform application-level checks, which centralizes operational policies. Fifth, maintenance becomes easier because servers can be taken out of rotation for upgrades while the load balancer continues to serve traffic from healthy nodes. An important operational note is that these benefits depend on good health checks and correct algorithm selection; a misconfigured health check or a poor algorithm choice can negate the advantages. For practical review, maintain a checklist to confirm horizontal scaling paths, health checks, graceful maintenance flows, and whether SSL termination or content routing should live on the balancer.

Choosing a load balancing algorithm shapes how requests land on backends and directly affects fairness and responsiveness. The main algorithms to know are Round Robin, Weighted Round Robin, Least Connection, Weighted Least Connection, IP Hash, and Least Time. Round Robin cycles requests sequentially through servers; it is simple and effective when servers are similar. Weighted Round Robin assigns more requests to stronger servers by giving them higher weights. Least Connection sends new requests to the server with the fewest active connections, which helps when requests vary in duration. Weighted Least Connection applies weights to that same idea. IP Hash computes a hash of the client’s IP so that the same client tends to reach the same server, which can provide session persistence without application cookies. Least Time is an advanced option that considers both response time and active connections to pick the fastest server. Use the three-server exercise from the chapter to practice: with servers handling 70, 30, and 50 active requests respectively, ask where the next five requests go under Round Robin versus Least Connection. A typical misconception is assuming Round Robin is always fair; it ignores current load and long-lived connections, which can make it unsuitable for heterogeneous or variable workloads. Your job as an architect is to match observed traffic patterns with the algorithm’s strengths and limitations.

Round Robin is one of the simplest load balancing strategies: forward each incoming request to the next server in the pool in a fixed sequence. Its simplicity is an advantage when servers are similar, but it ignores current load and request duration. Weighted Round Robin refines this by assigning weights to servers; a server with weight two receives twice as many requests as a server with weight one. Consider the chapter scenario where Server B is upgraded to handle more capacity — under Weighted Round Robin you would give B a higher weight so it receives proportionally more traffic. When assigning weights, base them on measurable capacity metrics such as C P U, memory, or network throughput. A common pitfall is choosing weights by gut feel rather than metrics, which can create imbalances. Another misconception is assuming Weighted Round Robin solves variable request durations — it helps for static capacity differences but still does not react to real-time connection counts or slow-running requests. For workloads with long-lived or highly variable requests, algorithms that consider active connections or response time are often better. Practice: pick capacity numbers for servers A, B, and C and calculate the assignment of the next 15 requests under Weighted Round Robin to confirm the expected distribution.

Least Connection algorithms route new requests to the backend with the fewest active connections. This is especially useful when requests have variable durations or when a server may be temporarily slower. Weighted Least Connection adds server capacity into the decision so faster backends still get more traffic but decisions remain informed by current load. Least Time is a more advanced choice: it factors in both active connections and measured response times to estimate which server will finish fastest for a new request. Why does this matter? In real-world services some requests are quick and some long-running; a purely sequential approach can overload a server processing many long requests. Least Connection dynamically compensates for that by steering new arrivals to less-busy servers. A common misconception is that counting connections equals perfect load measurement; long-lived idle connections can distort the view, and connection count doesn't capture C P U or input and output saturation. Always combine these algorithms with good health checks and real metrics like response latency and server utilization. A practical exercise is to simulate variable-duration requests and observe how Least Connection rebalances more effectively than Round Robin in that scenario.

IP Hash uses the client’s source IP address to compute a deterministic mapping to a backend server, providing a simple form of session persistence often called sticky sessions. This is useful when you need a client to reach the same server across multiple requests but cannot rely on application-level cookies. For example, a legacy web application that stores session state in local memory benefits from IP Hash because it keeps a client bound to a single backend. However, there are important limitations: clients behind NAT or large-scale proxies may share public IP addresses so affinity can become coarse or incorrect. Also, IP-based mapping can prevent even distribution when client IPs cluster in ranges. A common misconception is that IP Hash is universally superior for persistence; in practice it is a tradeoff that works well for straightforward topologies but not for complex, multi-tiered deployments or widespread NAT. When persistence is needed at scale, architects often use centralized session stores or application-level mechanisms combined with cookie-based affinity. The key is to weigh the simplicity of IP Hash against its affinity limitations in your environment.

HAProxy is a high-performance, open-source proxy and load balancer used widely in Red Hat environments. It handles both Layer 4 (TCP) and Layer 7 (HTTP) traffic, making it flexible for many workloads. HAProxy performs core functions such as connection multiplexing, application-layer health checks, SSL offloading, sticky sessions, and content-based routing. Architects pick HAProxy when they need a reliable, configurable component that can handle a large number of concurrent connections with predictable behavior. Typical deployments put HAProxy in front of web servers, application servers, or even databases, with backends forming a server farm. Important operational considerations include tuning for maximum connections, configuring appropriate health checks to detect real failures, and planning certificate management for SSL termination. A misconception is that HAProxy is only useful for HTTP; it is equally effective for TCP-based applications. When combined with a VIP manager such as Keepalived, HAProxy forms the distribution layer while Keepalived ensures the load balancer endpoint remains available. Practice sketching a deployment where HAProxy routes traffic to three app servers and performs an HTTP health check with a short interval so you can see how it removes unhealthy nodes quickly.
